Favouritism is the act or practice of giving special, unearned advantages or preferential treatment to a particular person or group, not because they have earned it or deserve it, but simply because of a personal connection, personal liking, or bias toward them. It is a form of unfair partiality.

Think of it this way. Imagine a teacher has 30 students in a class. One of them is her nephew. Even when her nephew submits poor work, she gives him high marks. Even when he misbehaves, she ignores it. Even when a more deserving student should be picked for an award, she picks her nephew. That teacher is showing favouritism.

Notice what is happening: she is not treating people based on what they have done or how they have performed. She is treating them based on who they are to her personally. That gap — the gap between what someone deserves and what they actually receive because of a personal connection — is exactly where favouritism lives.

This is the most important thing to understand. Not all preferential treatment is favouritism. A manager who gives a pay rise to the employee who worked the hardest is showing preference, but it is earned preference — it is fair. Favouritism is specifically the kind of preference that bypasses fairness entirely.

Three conditions are usually present when favouritism is occurring:

There is a position of power or influence involved. Favouritism requires someone who has the ability to give advantages — a boss, a teacher, a judge, a parent, a government official.

The advantage being given is something others could or should also be competing for equally — a job, a promotion, a prize, an opportunity, resources, or protection.

The reason for giving the advantage is personal — a friendship, a family relationship, a shared background, a personal liking — rather than merit, qualification, or fair criteria.

When all three are present, you have favouritism.
Where Favouritism Appears in Real Life

Favouritism is not confined to one setting. It can appear almost anywhere there is power and relationships coexisting.

In the workplace, a manager might hire a friend who is less qualified than other candidates, or give a cousin a promotion they did not earn, or assign the best projects only to people they personally like. Other employees are left at a disadvantage through no fault of their own.

In schools and universities, a teacher or professor might grade a favourite student more generously, overlook their rule-breaking, or pick them for opportunities regardless of ability. Other students who work just as hard or harder are passed over.

In families, a parent might consistently favour one child over others — giving them more freedom, more resources, more praise, or more support, not based on need or circumstance, but simply out of personal preference. This is sometimes called playing favourites.

In government and politics, favouritism takes the form of politicians awarding contracts, positions, or public resources to allies, donors, or friends rather than to whoever is most qualified or most deserving. This overlaps closely with corruption.

In sports, a referee or judge might make decisions that consistently benefit a particular player or team because of personal bias, not based on what actually happened in the game.

In social groups, a person in a leadership role — say, a club president or a community organiser — might distribute responsibilities, recognition, or benefits to people they are close to, while equally capable people on the outside of that inner circle are overlooked.

People do not always show favouritism out of malicious intent. Often, it is driven by deeply natural human tendencies that, when left unchecked, become unfair.

Human beings are naturally more comfortable with, and more trusting of, people who are similar to them, familiar to them, or personally close to them. This is a psychological tendency sometimes called in-group bias. We instinctively want to help the people we like and care about.

In many cases, favouritism is not even conscious. A manager might genuinely believe they are choosing the best candidate, when in reality their liking for that person is subtly colouring their judgement. This unconscious form is sometimes harder to address than the deliberate kind.

Other times, favouritism is entirely deliberate — a person knows exactly what they are doing and chooses to prioritise their personal relationships over fairness because it benefits them, their family, or their social circle.

Favouritism causes real harm, and understanding those harms helps explain why it is considered a serious flaw in any system, relationship, or institution.

It creates deep resentment and a sense of injustice among those who are treated less favourably. When people see that outcomes are determined not by effort or ability but by personal connections, they feel that their contributions are worthless — because in that context, they are.

It damages the overall quality of outcomes. When the best person for a job, a role, or a prize is routinely passed over in favour of someone's personal favourite, the results are worse for everyone. Organisations that run on favouritism tend to perform poorly because they are not putting their best people in their best positions.

It erodes trust. Once people recognise that a system is driven by favouritism, they lose faith in it. A court where judges show favouritism is not a court anyone can trust. A school where teachers show favouritism is not a place where students can feel they will be judged fairly.

It reinforces inequality. Favouritism tends to perpetuate advantage for those who are already connected, already in the inner circle, already close to power — and it keeps disadvantaged people further out.
Favouritism vs. Fair Preference — An Important Distinction

It is worth being clear on this, because the line can sometimes seem blurry.

Choosing the most qualified candidate for a job is not favouritism — it is fair selection. Giving a prize to the student with the best essay is not favouritism — it is merit-based reward. Even choosing to spend more time helping someone who is genuinely struggling more than others is not favouritism — it is a reasonable, justified response to a real difference in need.

Favouritism only occurs when the preferential treatment is not justified by any fair, reasonable, or objective standard. The moment personal connection overrides fair criteria, favouritism begins.

Similarly, having personal opinions and preferences about people is entirely human and not inherently wrong. The problem arises when a person in a position of power or influence allows those personal preferences to distort decisions that should be based on something more objective — merit, need, qualification, or fairness.

Nepotism is a specific, named form of favouritism that refers exclusively to favouring family members — giving jobs, positions, or advantages to relatives simply because they are relatives, regardless of their ability.

Cronyism is another specific form in which a person in power favours their close friends or allies — often in professional or political contexts — over more qualified or deserving candidates.

Both nepotism and cronyism are types of favouritism, but favouritism itself is the broader, more general term that covers all forms of unjust preferential treatment, regardless of whether the person being favoured is a family member, a friend, or simply someone the powerful person likes.

Bias is a related but slightly different concept. Bias refers to a leaning or tendency toward or against something. Favouritism can be the result of bias — particularly unconscious bias — but bias does not always lead to favouritism. You can hold a bias internally without it affecting your decisions. Favouritism is when bias (or simple personal preference) actually changes how you treat people.

Favouritism, in its simplest form, is this: treating someone better than others not because they deserve it, but because you personally like them, know them, or are connected to them. It is preference without justification — partiality without fairness. It appears in workplaces, schools, families, governments, and social groups. It causes resentment, damages quality, erodes trust, and deepens inequality. It is driven by natural human instincts that, when unchecked by fairness and accountability, turn into a practice that is widely regarded as unjust. Its close relatives are nepotism (favouring family) and cronyism (favouring allies), but favouritism itself is the overarching term for all such unjustified preferential treatment.
